California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

It has been revealed that but California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” mentioned Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, stated House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

According to recent reports, leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

Recent findings suggest that california Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Recent findings suggest that working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she noted. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido mentioned. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

It has been revealed that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

Sources indicate that the candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez noted. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

Industry observers note that amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

    #191464. Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television reveals, and more.
    • Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s newly introduced film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop.
    • Loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that on Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television reveals, and more. This time, we take a look at Fjord.

    Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s newly introduced film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop. The Romanian New Wave director won his second Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival for the Norway-set film, which is also his first shot outside of his home country and Romania’s official selection for the best international feature category at the 2027 Oscars.

    Loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children. Their conservative lifestyle soon puts them at odds with their progressive neighbors, and they find themselves in a custody battle after child abuse allegations surface, setting up a complicated debate between two opposing cultures and worldviews.

    Cristian Mungiu’s latest film is based on a real-life court case.

    Sources indicate that the film was shot over 36 days in spring 2025 in Western Norway’s Hjørundfjorden. The dramatic and mostly tourist-free fjord near the city of Ålesund cuts through the Sunnmøre Alps, with peaks rising up to 5,600 feet directly from the water.

    For the family home, location scouts selected a tiny village called Stenes, comprising just a few rustic buildings scattered on the shores of the fjord’s Norangsfjorden arm. Nearby, they shot church scenes at a simple wooden structure in the town of Øye with school scenes taking place in Sæbø and courthouse scenes being filmed in the “massive city” of Ålesund.

    Recent findings suggest that as the title of the film suggests, the fjord is more than just a mere setting—it’s a poetic space suffused with symbolic meaning for Mungiu. “I was attracted by this idea of a very secluded community where people can’t avoid finally talking to one another,” Mungiu claims. “The fjord evokes for me this need for solidarity among people when confronted with extreme coldness and severe weather.”.

    Mungiu sought to balance the epic scale of the fjord setting with the legal drama of the film.

    While audiences might expect the grandeur of a fjord to humble the people who live within it, in this movie, Mungiu instead uses the geographical formation to highlight their folly. “Normally, in front of nature’s force, people should become conscious of their fragility,” Mungiu says, “but too often their huge egos make them forget how mortal and insignificant they are, and they end up investing all their energy into imposing their point of view on others.”.

    In a recent development, the landscape worked particularly well within the context of Mungiu’s unique visual storytelling style: He conceives of each scene as a single shot, without cuts or close-ups, letting his characters move through expansive frames. As he describes it, “Every shot needs to be perfectly balanced in terms of light, interpretation, choreography, rhythm.” For this project, he imagined scenes that would call to mind the winter landscapes of Flemish Renaissance master Pieter Bruegel the Elder, who painted small human figures dwarfed by snowy scenery. The wide shots, Mungiu claims, “allow the majestic nature to feel a bit intimidating and menacing.”.

    The winter landscapes in the film were inspired by the work of Flemish Renaissance painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

    When it came time to select the perfect fjord, Mungiu was purely pragmatic. “I imagine scenes quite in detail when I write the screenplay and while scouting,” he explains. “I try to find locations as close as possible to what I’ve imagined.” He drew a “very precise sketch” for his location scout of what he was looking for: two neighboring houses at the end of a fjord, “with mountains and forests behind, quiet deep water in front, and a narrow road connecting them to the rest of the world—all this ideally covered in snow during wintertime.”.

    Industry observers note that his production team found a spot that looked just as he envisioned in Stenes, deep down the fjord and away from the coast, to maximize the potential for more snow. Then the hardest part started: convincing the homeowners to rent their properties out for the shoot.

    “Once we started our scouting, we felt that we were visiting a form of paradise,” he says. “The light always comes from an angle, the air is pure, the colors are strong, the calm of the ocean is threatening, the snow on the peaks looks menacing.” Everything in the area, he continues, “is clean, organized, precise, logical, and functional.” Mungiu jokes, “For an OCD person like me, it was the perfect place.”.

    Of course, the wildness of the fjord came with its own set of challenges, from avalanche warnings to a lack of consistent snow cover (they trucked in powder from the mountains). But Mungiu and his team tried to use these challenges to their artistic advantage. On the first day of shooting, for instance, a major storm forced them to move production inside and shoot an emotionally complex scene. Inspired by the dramatic gusts, they hung an enormous Norwegian flag just outside the window to thrash and snap in the gale, “adding a visual element to the inner feelings of Lisbet in a very delicate moment for her as a character.”.

    According to recent reports, the primary gateway town for the fjord is Ålesund, a coastal city known for its abundant Art Nouveau architecture. While it’s only about 20 miles from Stenes as the crow flies, the journey takes about two hours of scenic driving and ferry crossings to get to the spots where the movie was shot.

    Sebastian Stan as Mihai Gheorghiu, the devout evangelical main character who relocates his family to the titular Norwegian fjord.

    It has been revealed that if you want to see the fjord for yourself, an ideal lodging option is the lovely Hotel Union Øye, which opened early for the season to host the cast. Now a member of Relais & Châteaux, the gingerbread-like hotel debuted in 1891 and over the decades has hosted the likes of Henrik Ibsen, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Edvard Grieg, who composed music on the piano in the salon.

    It’s also possible to visit Hjørundfjorden on one of Norway’s most iconic journeys: a sailing with Hurtigruten, which is part pleasure cruise line, part local passenger ferry, and part cargo vessel for remote communities. In 2027, the line’s Coastal Express route, which hugs the coast from Bergen in the south to Kirkenes in the north, will visit Hjørundfjorden in May and September, while the Svalbard Line will make a stop at Sæbø in the fjord from May through September. (In the film’s Ålesund-set courtroom scenes, you can even see the ferry looming outside the windows.).

    Havila Voyages, a family-run Hurtigruten competitor, also stops in Hjørundfjorden seasonally from September 1 to October 31; optional excursions include a scenic drive through the surrounding countryside and mountain valleys; an e-bike tour through the narrow Norangsdalen valley along the “Queen’s Route” (so named because it was supposedly visited by seven queens); or a guided hike to a mountain dairy farm, followed by a snack of a svele (crepe).

    Sources indicate that and if you can’t make it to Norway, Mungiu is presenting an exhibition of his photographs from scouting trips and the film’s production called Fjord. The Pictures at Fresh York’s Romanian Cultural Institute in New York (through November 30). His images, all shot on a phone, depict the landscapes, people, architecture, and even weather that helped shape the film’s visual language.

    #191463. Latest Update: The Best German Christmas Markets Are Straight Out of a Fairy Tale

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (965 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Best German Christmas Markets Are Straight Out of a Fairy Tale

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You don’t have to travel to Munich or Nuremberg to get into the Christmas spirit and enjoy some lebkuchen or pfeffernüsse.
    • The façades of the houses on Bad Tölz’s Marktstraße glow with festive lights in the evening.
    • Industry observers note that in Bavaria’s Bad Tölz, a medieval town sitting on the Isar River, the scent of roasted almonds mingles with the sound of Christmas carols, while the historic market square is decorated with garlands and wreaths.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You don’t have to travel to Munich or Nuremberg to get into the Christmas spirit and enjoy some lebkuchen or pfeffernüsse. The streets of the country’s small towns are also filled with holiday cheer that’s best experienced at their Christmas markets. Amid their narrow alleys and on cobblestone squares, there’s a special atmosphere every December. Here’s our selection of seven to visit this season.

    The façades of the houses on Bad Tölz’s Marktstraße glow with festive lights in the evening.

    Industry observers note that in Bavaria’s Bad Tölz, a medieval town sitting on the Isar River, the scent of roasted almonds mingles with the sound of Christmas carols, while the historic market square is decorated with garlands and wreaths. At the Christmas market, approximately 40 festively decorated stalls are set up right in front of the historic façades of the old town. The atmosphere is especially magical in the evening hours when the Christmas lights sparkle everywhere. For children, there’s a carousel, a curated program of activities, and the popular Family Wednesdays with discounts and carriage rides.

    According to recent reports, hours: 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, from November 27 to December 23, 2026; 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on December 24.

    Industry observers note that the Wernigerode Christmas Market is set against the backdrop of some of the historic buildings in this town in the Harz Mountains. Snow often covers the roofs, and Christmas carols fill the air at the popular event.

    According to recent reports, hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m.; from November 20 to December 22, 2026.

    The medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber is even more magical than usual during the Christmas season.

    It has been revealed that in the pre-Christmas season, the medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber, located on the Romantic Road in Bavaria, becomes even more enchanting. The opening of the market is a small spectacle when, on the Friday before the first Sunday of Advent, the large Christmas tree on the market square is illuminated in a festive ceremony. The town’s Christmas market continues a tradition with more than 500 years of history. In the narrow alleys and squares near the town hall, including the market square, visitors will find everything they could desire as they embrace the Christmas season: from gifts like handmade jewelry to freshly baked gingerbread. The Christmas Village, a nearly 11,000-square-foot store located not far from the Market Square, continues the holiday spirit year-round.

    Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; from November 20 to December 23, 2026, closed November 23.

    A special feature of the Gengenbach Advent Market is the window-opening ritual which transforms the town hall into an enormous advent calendar.

    In a recent development, one of the things that makes the Gengenbach Advent Market in the Black Forest stand out is its window-opening ritual. On December 1, the town hall transforms into the world’s largest Advent calendar with a unique art display. Every evening at 6 p.m., one of 24 windows opens. In each one there’s a work of art, often by world-renowned artists such as Marc Chagall and Andy Warhol. Visitors from all over the world come to Gengenbach to see this unique calendar against the romantic backdrop of the historic old town.

    Hours: Monday to Friday, 2 p.m. to 8 p.m.; Saturdays and Sundays, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. From November 27 to December 23, 2026.

    Quedlinburg is already a World Heritage City, but during the Christmas season it becomes even more romantic.

    Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Fridays, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.; Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.. From November 25 to December 22, 2026.

    An enchanting setting and a varied program are the draws at the Bernkastel-Kues Christmas Market.

    A torch-lit swim, fireworks, and a hike with St. Nicholas: During Advent, the Christmas market in Bernkastel-Kues, a town in a famous winegrowing town near the borders with Luxembourg and Belgium, offers a program of activities that few can match. Torch-lit swimmers bravely plunge into the cold, wintry Moselle on December 5, and both children and adults can join St. Nicholas on a hike on December 6. (The route varies each year, but it always begins at the market square and typically covers between six and nine miles.) This year marks the 48th time the historic old town has served as the backdrop for this romantic Christmas market. Amid half-timbered façades and cobblestone streets, stalls offer traditional crafts, gift ideas, and delicious treats.

    It has been revealed that hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. From November 20 to December 20, 2026, closed November 22.

    Small and charming, but also very brief: The Meersburg Christmas Market is open for only two days.

    Recent findings suggest that admittedly, a weekend isn’t much time to experience the Christmas market in the old town of Meersburg, on the shores of Lake Constance (Bodensee) in southwestern Germany. But with some carefully planning, you can make the most of the time you have. Both days are packed with Christmas activities, ranging from barrel organ music to readings and puppet shows for the youngest visitors. The stalls sell handicrafts, regional products, and Christmas treats. The market in the castle park is a highlight. And because the event is so short, it makes it all the more special with all the holiday fun concentrated in just two days.

    In a recent development, hours: 3 p.m. to 9 p.m., Friday, November 27, and 2 p.m. to 8 p.m., Saturday, November 28, 2026.

    This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller Germany.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

    But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

    Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

    We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

    The answer was a resounding yes.

    Recent findings suggest that mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

    Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

    In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

    They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:.

    Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a new card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

    By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a latest one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

    The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

    Next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

    Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

    However, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a latest card to diversify her rewards?

    With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a new card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

    And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

    She’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her newly introduced card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

    “I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table.".

    Industry observers note that our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

    Industry observers note that while Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

    Denver opted for a new cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

    She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

    After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

    One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”.

    In a recent development, everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

    One went with a upcoming travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

    All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

    This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

    Don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

    #191460. 19 Best Resorts in California, From Pebble Beach to Napa Valley

    📅 07 Aug 2020 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3053 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    19 Best Resorts in California, From Pebble Beach to Napa Valley

    📅 07 Aug 2020 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in the late 1800s, travelers arriving on the West Coast found that the gold rush had dried up, but another kind of treasure was waiting in its wake: the health spa.
    • Of course, it’s a massive state with hundreds of different landscapes, so finding the right resort is all about knowing what makes you come alive.
    • Recent findings suggest that auberge Collection’s third property in Napa Valley is set on a historic Wine Country ranch founded in 1856 by Judge Edward Stanly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in the late 1800s, travelers arriving on the West Coast found that the gold rush had dried up, but another kind of treasure was waiting in its wake: the health spa. Soon, doctors back east were prescribing trips to the Golden State for ailing patients in search of restorative sunshine, mineral springs, and fresh air. California’s reputation as a destination for serious R&R has persisted ever since. From beachfront properties in SoCal to redwood hideaways along the Significant Sur coast to vineyardside estates in Napa Valley, the best resorts in California are a kind of gold standard all their own.

    Of course, it’s a massive state with hundreds of different landscapes, so finding the right resort is all about knowing what makes you come alive. Looking to spend time on the links? There are legendary fairways waiting at Pebble Beach. Craving an off-the-grid escape? Decamp to a secluded sanctuary in the Santa Rosa Mountains. Prefer five-star amenities with near-clairvoyant service, or a home base for wine tastings and lavish dining? Consider it covered. Read on for the best resorts in California, where the good life is the real gold rush.

    Recent findings suggest that auberge Collection’s third property in Napa Valley is set on a historic Wine Country ranch founded in 1856 by Judge Edward Stanly. Guests can choose from 135 cottages, rooms, and suites—decorated in oatmeal and beige hues with leather and oak furnishings—all with private terraces and outdoor showers. Standout amenities include Guatemalan heated robes, yoga mats, and Theragun massage tools. Bay Area food lovers make the trek here just to sample chef Anthony Stagnaro’s ingredient-focused meals at the resort’s Avroko-designed restaurant, Bear; others prefer to sip rosé at the French countryside-inspired Basin Bar or order a scoop of ice cream at The Window. But don’t expect to drink wine all day: This wellness-focused resort can curate fitness optimization programs, send you out on a cycling adventure with a pro, or arrange a hot-air balloon ride for the whole family. —Jen Murphy.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    While it’s tempting to paint Sonoma as a sleepy sweep of California Wine Country, the truth is, the county is every bit as—if not more—booming than neighboring Napa. It’s got Michelin-starred restaurants, shiny newly introduced tasting rooms, and significant-name hotels cropping up on the regular. But to try a little of that sweet Sonoma of yesteryear, there’s no better place than Farmhouse Inn. Located near the Russian River—and within easy driving distance to charming Healdsburg, as well as some of the region's best vineyards—this 25-room property feels delightfully laid-back and intimate. The Inn has five different room categories, all with a country-chic look; bright and airy with white wainscoting, pillowy bedding, and haute-rustic touches that might include a personal welcome message on a small blackboard, a fireplace, and comfortable overstuffed chairs. The Farmhouse Restaurant occupies a beautiful space and offers an ever-evolving chef’s tasting menu with hyper-local ingredients paired with, naturally, a stellar regional wine list. All in all, Farmhouse Inn looks and feels like a classic New England country charmer—with California Wine Country street cred. —Rebecca Misner.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that this outstanding Napa Valley hotel is set on 33 acres of vineyards and olive groves—needless to say, the views are spectacular. Sumptuous cottages done in sun and earth tones have wood-burning fireplaces and refrigerators stocked with local wines and cheeses; bathrooms come with skylights and flat-screen TVs. The restaurant serves Wine Country cuisine with French and Mediterranean influences, and its terrace has heaters for dining out on cool evenings. Enjoy Italian ices and chilled towels at the pool and Reiki at La Pagode, an Asian-style pavilion. —Todd Plummer.

    Recent findings suggest that napa has a handful of excellent hotels and no shortage of fabulous wineries and tasting rooms, but this is the first full-on luxury resort that marries the two. The property’s 85 rooms and suites, as well as 20 private residences, are surrounded by acres of vineyards. The bar and dining space are gorgeous—soaring ceilings, a glassed-in kitchen, and a wall of glass doors that open onto a huge terrace with a firepit—but made cozy by comfy booths and warm lighting. The on-site winery and its tasting room are another way this resort stands out. It’s a dream to walk from your room to a tasting and not have to worry about driving or calling a car. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that northern California’s Wine Country retreats often model themselves on faraway places; destinations with longer traditions and more old-world gravitas. This is too bad, because their location, between the Pacific and the Mayacamas Mountains, is pure magic, and by this point on the domestic wine timeline, there’s no need to apologize for who you are. This is why the arrival of Montage’s first property in the region, and Sonoma’s first large-scale luxury resort, was so exciting when it opened in 2020. It celebrates its own landscape, leaving the 22,000 live oaks in place and pulling a palette of dun and moss from the surrounding sun-soaked vineyards. The restaurant offers a bounty of Sonoma’s best, with everything—from the Pliny the Elder IPA to the lamb shank—sourced from within miles. And the local sixth-generation vintners who frequent the sprawling patio bar are happy to remind you that there is, in fact, plenty of history in these parts. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that there are golf resorts, and then there’s Casa Palmero at Pebble Beach. The course, Pebble Beach Golf Links, opened more than 100 years ago in 1919, and has enjoyed as long and storied a history as any. The resort, a former private residence that opened in 1999, is directly on the course—rooms overlook the first and second fairways—making it an absolute dream for golfers. But Casa Palmero offers so much more than tee times. The rooms have a countryside vibe—spacious with wood-burning fireplaces, exposed ceiling beams, and wrought-iron fixtures—while the Spa at Pebble Beach offers award-winning service. Plus, it’s only a five-minute walk down to the peaceful beach.

    Set on 500 acres in the foothills of the Santa Lucia Mountains along California’s Central Coast, Carmel Valley Ranch is located just shy of 13 miles from the Monterey Bay Aquarium and historic Cannery Row. At check-in, you’ll receive a list of the resort’s scheduled activities, and staff will likely share their favorites—and you should pay attention. Options range from guided hikes and yoga to archery lessons and picnics with Pablo and Paco, a pair of resident miniature donkeys. There are also multiple pools, tennis and pickleball courts, and an 18-hole Pete Dye–designed golf course. If the blinds are up at the on-site creamery, stopping by the window to watch the cheesemaker in action is a must. Along with chickens and a salt house, the organic garden is home to veggies, flowers, and honeybees. Menus at signature restaurant Valley Kitchen showcase fresh, local ingredients—many of which are grown or produced on the resort. —Dana Rebmann.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that this beloved Major Sur resort, which dramatically overlooks the Pacific and is surrounded by acres of forest, received a total reboot in 2025. And while it may look new—rooms have all been updated with plenty of wood and neutrals, 15 luxe safari-style tents have been added to the roster, and the spa got a relaxation deck that looks out at the ocean—it hasn't lost its laid-back 1970s vibe. It's still, hands down, one of the most magical places to disconnect and get back in touch with nature. —Christina Ohly Evans.

    Sources indicate that the Post Ranch Inn is a total immersion in the singular landscape of Significant Sur, in environs defined by a sense of understated luxury. The Ranch’s 40 rooms have all been designed to both blend in with and have a light touch upon the land, and range from tree houses to clifftop suites with expansive views of the mountains to the east or, better yet, the ocean’s expanse to the west. Engage with the environment some more by exploring the property’s hiking trails, taking a tour of the chef’s garden, or signing up for a falconry lesson. —Lauren Sloss.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    It might seem like a mistake to go to Santa Barbara and not stay close to the shore, but the moment you make the turn inland onto San Ysidro Road, you realize that being here isn’t about visiting Santa Barbara; it’s about visiting the ranch. Just 38 cottages, each with its own unique layout, decor, and view, are spread out over 550 acres, but rather than being scattered, they form a ring within the property. At the resort’s center is a collection of gardens as well as a rectangular pool that overlooks the canyon. Some of the curated finds you’ll see throughout are museum-quality art, antiques sourced from the owner’s world travels, and handmade wallpapers. But San Ysidro Ranch isn’t your typical hotel—as its history of having legendary guests like Jacqueline and John F. Kennedy, who honeymooned here, or John Huston, who finished writing the screenplay for The African Queen on the property, can attest. It continues its legacy as a celebrity refuge, as modern-day A-listers use this tucked-away spot to truly hide out and escape—which is what you should do too. —Samantha Brooks.

    This is the original Hollywood hideaway with seven acres of land nestled in the foothills of the American Riviera. At El Encanto, you’ll have views overlooking the Pacific Coast with the rose-colored mountains rising behind you. The property has 90 rooms, but it never feels crowded; in fact, it feels private and idyllic. It has a fantastic luxe Spanish colonial charm without being annoying or precious. Whether you’re hiding away in a lush garden suite with a fireplace and a patio or just swanning around on the terrace for an alfresco farmers market lunch, it feels just right: low-key but ultra stylish. Call it what it is: a retreat. —Daniel Scheffler.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Arriving at Rosewood Miramar Beach, with its military-straight rows of white roses and pristine clapboard cottages, feels like landing on a postcard-perfect street in Cape Cod. If it all seems a little too perfect, well, there was time to get things right. The former Miramar by the Sea Hotel occupied these 16 oceanfront acres from 1889 until it closed for renovations in 2000. The hotel sat half-demolished for years, its second act tangled in red tape. It took SoCal billionaire developer Rick Caruso and the Hong Kong–based Rosewood Hotel Group to push the project through. And while it may have been tempting to scrap the past after such a treacherous road to reopening, the new Miramar deliberately throws back. Lemon-yellow-and-white striped umbrellas flank a rectangular pool where the Scoop Shop serves up fountain drinks, ice cream cones, and burgers. Overlooking the ocean, there’s Caruso’s, the type of place where you order a martini with your cacio e pepe alongside a heaping dollop of la dolce vita (the chef hails from Harry’s Bar in Rome)—and, in a state where “formal flip-flops" are a thing, one that blessedly enforces a dress code. In case you start to feel too lost in the 1950s, an outpost from Malibu Farm and a Goop boutique remind you that this is indeed modern-day Cali. —R.M.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    Time slows down as you drive down the oversized, oak-tree-lined driveway at Alisal Ranch. Immediately upon checking in, you're greeted with countryside hospitality that makes you feel like you're light-years away from LA. The rooms are furnished with just the right amount of country Western kitsch, complete with wood-burning fireplaces, Pendleton blankets, and vintage paintings, and the beds are incredibly comfy—the perfect spot to rest your head after a day of adventuring. The highlight of your weekend will undoubtedly be horseback riding through groves of oaks up to the pancake breakfast. And the bar deserves a nod too, with a giant fireplace that makes for the perfect spot to enjoy a whiskey neat. —K.S.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    Sources indicate that to book a stay at this impeccably designed escape, guests must send an inquiry through the website—a sign of just how exclusive the hotel is. The reward is an extremely private getaway with a relaxing, neutral design and an incredible Nobu restaurant. Opened in April 2017, this serene escape was once a 1950s-era beach motel. Now, it's a study in high-design restraint—which is clear after setting one foot inside its almost hidden entrance. Guests enter through a courtyard that looks out onto the ocean, which leads to a beautiful garden. Follow the path to a deck made from ipe wood that overlooks Carbon Beach and Malibu Pier. —Brooke Porter Katz.

    Check Availability at Tripadvisor.

    In a recent development, montage Laguna Beach is a polished, residential-style resort set on 30 oceanfront acres along one of Southern California’s most scenic stretches of coastline. Opened in 2003 as the brand’s flagship, the hotel continues to deliver consistent high-level service, a strong food and beverage program, and a true sense of privacy despite its size. Every one of the 263 rooms has an ocean view and outdoor space, and the property's layout, from the cliffside paths, tiered lawns, and access to Treasure Island Beach, makes it easy to settle in and stay awhile. Guests skew toward special-occasion travelers, West Coast couples, families, and loyal Montage regulars who return year after year. Highlights include the 20,000-square-foot Spa Montage, the renovated Mosaic Pool, direct beach access, and the return of Studio Mediterranean, the resort’s stellar fine-dining venue. While there’s no tennis or golf on-site, the concierge can arrange access at a nearby club. —Michelle Gross.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Time seems to slow down as you pull up to this sprawling Spanish revival hotel. Birds chirp from atop the towering oak trees, and the peaceful running fountains set the tone for a zen-like serenity that'll carry through your weekend. The rooms are personal retreats, many with soaking tubs, hand-painted Spanish tile, gold-auburn granite, and cobalt blue accents that give a modern Mediterranean look. Some rooms even have stucco fireplaces with seating, the perfect spot to tuck into a book and indulge in the rejuvenating spirit of Ojai. If that's not enough for you, the pools here are worth the visit alone—attentive staff, killer views, and plenty of space to hop around to keep the scenery fresh. —Krista Simmons.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Toeing the line between self-improvement sabbatical and bona fide vacation, Sensei Porcupine Creek is the ideal getaway for the chronic over-achiever: a place where real R&R is achieved proactively, through science and strategy, and in utter seclusion. Formerly the private estate of tech wizard and Silicon Valley billionaire Larry Ellison, Sensei’s co-founder, this intensely isolated retreat hidden in the foothills of the Santa Rosa Mountains is the second outpost for Sensei, and it marked the brand’s debut in the continental United States. (Its first, Sensei Lānaʻi, A Four Seasons Resort, opened in 2019.) But it’s also the brand’s first true standalone property, and with a lush, 75-acre golf course, a glamorous lagoon-style pool, and tennis facilities modeled after those at the nearby Indian Wells Tennis Garden—which hosts the annual BNP Paribas Tennis Tournament—it really does stand alone. —Betsy Blumenthal.

    The Resort at Pelican Hill, located in the ultra-exclusive Newport Coast zip code, has a luxurious Tuscan vibe, with well-manicured hills overlooking the Pacific, beautiful villas and bungalows, and Roman aqueduct–style architecture. At 504 acres, it's huge—so huge that you'll likely need your car to get to your room. It's also surrounded by 50,000 acres of protected green spaces. You'll want to leave plenty of time to relax by the Coliseum Pool, the resort's crown jewel. —Archana Ram.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    In a recent development, this sprawling getaway is peak California. Think orange groves, bright pink bougainvillea, and Spanish Colonial architecture. The main features—the suites, restaurants, lobby—are spread out across 45 acres, making it feel more like a luxurious neighborhood than a typical resort. Located in Rancho Santa Fe, a ritzy enclave 25 miles north of downtown San Diego, this place has the whole package—beautiful decor, dedicated service, next-level amenities, well-manicured grounds, and a serene vibe. —Jennie Nunn.

    Check Availability at Mr and Mrs Smith.

    What is the best luxury resort in California?

    Recent findings suggest that san Ysidro Ranch, at the foot of the Santa Ynez Mountains, is one of the best resorts in the world, let alone California. The property sprawls across 550 acres of citrus groves, gardens, and hiking trails, and each of its 38 rooms is a luxury cottage with a stone fireplace and antique furnishings that reflect its 130+ year history. Dignitaries like Winston Churchill, Audrey Hepburn, and Lucille Ball have stayed here—not to mention JFK and Jackie Kennedy, who called it their honeymoon hotel in 1953.

    What is the best place to visit in California if you're a first-time visitor?

    California is so varied that it’s hard to pick a favorite zone, but there are few places in the world like Big Sur, where redwoods tower overhead and dramatic cliffs drop to the Pacific below. It can be a bit rustic, but that’s a big part of the charm.

    What is the difference between a hotel and resort?

    Recent findings suggest that A hotel is mainly a place to sleep. A resort is the destination itself. Resorts typically sit on larger grounds and bundle the amenities you’d otherwise have to leave to find, like spas, pools, golf, multiple restaurants, and organized activities, so you can spend your whole stay on-property. In California, that might mean a round of golf at Pebble Beach before dinner, or a day of hiking, a massage, and a wine tasting without needing to hop in your car.

    How we choose the best resorts in California.

    Industry observers note that every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

    Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move rapidly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move rapidly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries noted, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    Industry observers note that the proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust fresh majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Fresh York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    In a recent development, democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    Without an confirmed challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have noted they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Sources indicate that rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries noted Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    According to recent reports, this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    According to recent reports, that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”.

    “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” stated Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley stated that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley remarked. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very firm that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    In a recent development, “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson remarked. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a manufacturer’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    According to recent reports, myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also remarked that Hawley’s fresh arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    In a recent development, “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    #191451. The US Air Force Bolted Jet Engines Onto Its Largest-Ever Bomber, But It Still Wasn't Enough To Save It

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1534 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The US Air Force Bolted Jet Engines Onto Its Largest-Ever Bomber, But It Still Wasn't Enough To Save It

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Convair B-36 Peacemaker strategic bomber is one of the most ambitious bombers ever built.
    • According to recent reports, this remained the case until newer all-jet bombers, particularly the B-52 Stratofortress, assumed the primary nuclear deterrence role.
    • The Convair B-36 Peacemaker was the largest bomber built by the US, and it can be thought of as the most crucial transitional bomber ever built.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Convair B-36 Peacemaker strategic bomber is one of the most ambitious bombers ever built. While the unusual pusher configuration of its six Pratt & Whitney R-4360 Wasp Major piston engines is perhaps its most distinctive feature, later variants also carried four General Electric J47 turbojets. These jets were added to improve take-off performance, climb rate, and high-speed dash capability, helping keep the enormous bomber operationally relevant.

    According to recent reports, this remained the case until newer all-jet bombers, particularly the B-52 Stratofortress, assumed the primary nuclear deterrence role. The United States Air Force procured 384 B-36s, each capable of carrying up to 86,000 lb (39,000 kg) of bombs. Although none remain airworthy today, four complete aircraft have been preserved in museums, where they provide a reminder of the largest piston-engined combat aircraft ever placed into operational service.

    The Convair B-36 Peacemaker was the largest bomber built by the US, and it can be thought of as the most crucial transitional bomber ever built. The US Air Force Museum states that "responding to the U.S. Army Air Forces' requirement for a strategic bomber with intercontinental range, Consolidated Vultee (later Convair) designed the B-36 during World War II. The airplane made its maiden flight in August 1946, and in June 1948 the Strategic Air Command received its first operational B-36.".

    The museum also explains that "some B-36s served as photographic reconnaissance aircraft, and others were adapted to launch and retrieve specially modified RF-84F/K reconnaissance planes." Although conceived during the Second World War as an ultra-long-range conventional bomber, the B-36 entered service as the United States shifted towards a strategy centred on delivering nuclear weapons across intercontinental distances without relying on overseas bases.

    This remains a central mission of the world's current strategic bombers (B-52, B-1B, B-2, B-21, Tu-160, and Tu-95MS). The Peacemaker's origins date to 1941, which is before the US even entered the Second World War. There was a fear in the US that the UK could fall to Germany, and if that happened, the US would lack a forward base for its bombers to raid Germany. As such, the requirements for the bomber included that it could fly intercontinentally from North America to Europe.

    Recent findings suggest that designing and developing the bomber took time, and by the time it entered service in 1948, the Second World War had been over for three years. As things had panned out, the US had been able to use Britain against Germany, and had island-hopped to bring its B-29s within range of Japan.

    However, the delays in designing the bomber also allowed engineers to upgrade the design to carry the heavy nuclear bombs that weighed around 8,800 to 11,000 lbs (4,000 to 5,000 kg) and even the extremely heavy hydrogen bombs. The first experimental thermonuclear devices weighed tens of tonnes, while the first operational hydrogen bombs introduced in the early 1950s typically weighed around 30,000–42,000 lb (14,000–19,000 kg).

    Convair B-36 Peacemaker Specs (Per US Air Force Museum).

    6x Pratt & Whitney R-4360 Wasp Major piston engines.

    4x General Electric J47 turbojets.

    It has been revealed that the Peacemaker was designed with the gigantic bomb bay doors needed to carry these bombs that no other aircraft could. When it entered service, it was able to carry around 86,000 lbs (39,000 kg) of payload, vastly more than any other bomber. With the establishment of the Strategic Air Command in 1946, the B-36 became the first true intercontinental nuclear bomber.

    In a recent development, the world's geostrategic picture changed in 1949 as the Soviet Union exploded its first atomic bomb. Then, the US pivoted to requiring a bomber able to strike targets deep inside the USSR while using bases in the continental United States and be able to carry heavy first-generation nuclear bombs. This is something the Boeing B-29 Superfortress couldn't do, but it was very similar to what the B-36 was originally designed for.

    Recent findings suggest that with the benefit of hindsight, the B-36 was always likely to be overtaken by the rapid pace of jet-powered aviation. It was conceived during the Second World War, but was ultimately built for a very different strategic environment. At first (late 1940s to early 1950s), the B-36 was unmatched.

    According to recent reports, no fighter could reliably intercept the Peacemaker at its high operating altitude (around 40,000 feet or 12,000 meters, later extending to 45,000 feet or 13,700 meters). This was before the USSR developed an integrated air defense network and a time when early Soviet jet fighters struggled to reach and engage such high-flying targets.

    It has been revealed that the Peacemaker's enormous range also allowed it to approach the USSR from multiple directions, further complicating interceptions. But the B-36 was becoming a relic of a bygone era. It was designed before jet-powered strategic bombers were practical. By the mid-1950s, newly introduced Soviet jet interceptors like the MiG-17 and then MiG-19 made it increasingly vulnerable.

    This worsened with the development of increasingly capable radar-guided air defense systems and surface-to-air missile technology. The arrival of the all-jet B-52 Stratofortress further hastened the B-36's retirement by offering greater speed, improved survivability, and comparable intercontinental range. Perhaps somewhat similar, the arrival of the B-21 will inevitably increase pressure to retire the older, expensive, and less survivable B-2 Spirits.

    By the time it entered service, the B-52 was in development, but was still years away. The Peacemaker was primarily powered by six enormous 28-cylinder Pratt & Whitney R-4360 Wasp Major piston engines arranged in a distinctive pusher configuration. However, these were too slow in the emerging jet age. In an effort to bridge the gap, the US Air Force invested heavily in modernizing the Peacemaker with four General Electric J47 turbojets.

    The J47 turbojet engines were mounted in two twin-engine pods beneath the outwings and earned it the famous slogan "six turning and four burning." They were not intended for continuous cruise as they were incredibly fuel inefficient. Instead, they were used for heavy-weight takeoffs, improved climbing, increased dash speed in hostile territory, and reduced time spent over defended targets.

    The USAF looked for other ways to improve the performance of the Peacemaker. It introduced the Featherweight modification programs, which removed defensive armament, ammunition, armor, and other equipment to improve altitude, range, and speed. The B-36 was given improved electronics, while the RB-36 strategic reconnaissance variant was also developed.

    The Air Force Museum states that "powered by six Pratt & Whitney R-4360 engines, the B-36J cruised at 230 mph [200 knots], but for additional bursts of speed its four General Electric J47s increased the maximum speed to 435 mph [378 knots]." Ultimately, the improvements addressed symptoms, but were unable to fix the underlying problem, which was that the B-36 just didn't belong in the jet age.

    It has been revealed that relying on piston engines, the B-36 was too slow, typically cruising at 200 knots (378 knots at maximum speed). The B-47 Stratojet could cruise at 434 knots, and the B-52 at 456 knots. By the mid-1950s, increasingly capable Soviet jet interceptors such as the MiG-17 and MiG-19, together with radar-guided surface-to-air missile systems including the S-25 Berkut and later the S-75 Dvina, steadily eroded the B-36's survivability.

    The Peacemaker faced other pressures. For example, the complex push-configuration radial engines frequently overheated, caught fire, and required changing a staggering 336 spark plugs per service. The massive size of the aircraft also demanded immense resources to maintain and operate.

    The final B-36 Peacemaker was retired in 1959, just one year before a Soviet S-75 Dvina (SA-2) downed a Lockheed U-2 spy plane at an altitude of around 70,000 feet. The development contributed to the program that would give rise to the SR-71 as well as contributed to the abandoning of the XB-70 Valkyrie bomber.

    Industry observers note that today, the Peacemaker is largely forgotten in popular memory. It is overshadowed by the earlier B-29 Superfortress, which entered service too late to make a difference in Germany but in time to play a pivotal role in ending the War in the Pacific, including dropping the nuclear bombs on Japan. The B-36 arrived too late for the Second World War, but it was also ill-prepared for the realities of the Cold War and the jet age.

    In a recent development, it was rapidly overshadowed by the early Cold War Boeing B-52 Stratofortress that entered service in the mid 1950s and continues in service today. These two successful bombers have had the effect of pushing the Peacemaker out of popular imagination. Unlike the B-29 and B-52, relatively few B-36s were preserved after retirement, with only four surviving in museums. None remain airworthy.

    Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    Sources indicate that these can be seen at the National Museum of the United States Air Force, Pima Air & Space Museum, Strategic Air Command & Aerospace Museum, and Castle Air Museum. Making matters worse for the Peacemaker is that it was never used in combat. It entered service after the Second World War, was absent from the Korean War, and had disappeared by the time of the Vietnam War, when the B-52s were very active.

    FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (284 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S.
    • If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.
    • Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

    If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

    Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

    Industry observers note that air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

    Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials stated they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

    “Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford noted in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more crucial than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”.

    Industry observers note that the FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

    #191449. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five fresh air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    In a recent development, they justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    According to recent reports, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., remarked the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Industry observers note that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott noted, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    According to recent reports, “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Sources indicate that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he remarked that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create complications in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford remarked Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    Industry observers note that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    According to recent reports, bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
