    Allegiant Air Ditches 26 Nonstop Routes: See Full List Now

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that it is critically key for an airline to know exactly what it is and isn't.
    • If Allegiant's network in Q1 2026 (January to March) is compared to what's available in the same three months in 2027, 26 routes have been removed.
    • Schedule analysis using OAG data indicates that all of the following markets saw the ULCC in Q1 2026 but will not do so in Q1 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that it is critically key for an airline to know exactly what it is and isn't. The ultra-low-cost carrier, Allegiant Air, knows the answer immediately. It is and always will be unashamedly a leisure-focused operator, with the acquisition of Sun Country by the Allegiant Travel Organization strengthening its position.

    If Allegiant's network in Q1 2026 (January to March) is compared to what's available in the same three months in 2027, 26 routes have been removed. Inevitably, some of them involve airports to which the airline no longer flies. Mostly, however, the links have simply been removed from still-served airports.

    Schedule analysis using OAG data indicates that all of the following markets saw the ULCC in Q1 2026 but will not do so in Q1 2027. Some may have had flights in January, February, and March this year, while others may have only had service in one or two of the months.

    20 of them have been removed entirely from Allegiant's map due to what is normal route churn. No flights are planned beyond the stated month. The remaining six markets are very different. While they won't be served in the first three months of the upcoming year, they'll simply return later in 2027. Some may say that including them is unfair, but they feature because two different time periods were compared.

    Routes (All Served In Q1 2026 But Not In Q1 2027).

    Bellingham to Los Angeles, Cincinnati to Los Angeles, Nashville to Peoria, Las Vegas to Boise.

    Fort Lauderdale to Traverse City, Orlando Sanford to Columbia.

    Bellingham to Palm Springs, Bellingham to Oakland, Fort Lauderdale to Columbia, Fort Lauderdale to Savannah, Fort Lauderdale to Tri-State/Huntington, Las Vegas to Chattanooga, Pittsburgh to Phoenix Sky Harbor, Punta Gorda to Fresh Orleans.

    Bellingham to Burbank, Las Vegas to Lexington, Nashville to Akron/Canton, Nashville to Sarasota (returns later in 2027), Portland to Idaho Falls, Washington Dulles to Savannah.

    Akron/Canton to Myrtle Beach (returns later in 2027), Boston to Des Moines (returns later in 2027), Denver to Knoxville (returns later in 2027), Denver to Peoria (returns later in 2027), Las Vegas to Asheville, Nashville to Gulf Shores (returns later in 2027).

    As Allegiant has pulled out of Columbia, Los Angeles International, Oakland, and Palm Springs, the quartet's last remaining routes in the examined period inevitably featured. Los Angeles International joined the carrier's network in 2009. In the past ten years alone, over 13,000 departures were available. It was the carrier's 18th most-served airport in this period.

    While the following links were served by Allegiant in the first three months of 2026, they will not have nonstop operations in the same quarter next year. They are not cut, as they'll all return in spring 2027. Most have simply become seasonal, which is, of course, designed to better align capacity with demand to improve yield and load factor performance.

    Comments About Q1 2026 Operations.

    Only 2 departures in January (they all count!), as an extension of winter operations until that month.

    15 departures in January, February, and March.

    8 departures in March, when the season resumed.

    Only 2 departures in January, as an extension of winter operations until that month.

    Only 1 departure in January, as an extension of winter operations until that month.

    8 departures in March, when the season resumed.

    Recent findings suggest that located in Alabama, not far from Mobile and Pensacola, Gulf Shores welcomed scheduled services a year and a half ago. Allegiant is currently the only operator there, although Sun Country will debut next year. The pair blueprint 14 routes in 2027, including Nashville.

    It has been revealed that the route from Tennessee had been on Allegiant's map since November 2025. Between then and August 2026, the load factor was a ridiculously low 64.7%. January and February were among the worst months, which is why flights do not resume until April. If things don't pick up, the route won't be coming back in 2028.

    At 1,585 nautical miles (2,935 km) each way, Allegiant had service between Las Vegas and Asheville from March 2021 until November 2026. Not surprisingly, it had two weekly flights, with both the 156-seat A319 and 186-seat A320 deployed. As is often the case, the market did not have nonstop flights until Allegiant's arrival.

    DOT data at the moment extends to August 2026. Between March 2021 and that summer month, Allegiant transported 162,157 round-trip passengers. It had 69% of the local market in this period, with the rest of the traffic flying via hubs with other operators. Allegiant filled 81.2% of the available seats, although the fares needed to achieve that result are unknown.

    Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees).
    • It has been revealed that in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

    It has been revealed that in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.

    Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:.

    Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most vital factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

    The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

    In terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who at the moment has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    It has been revealed that beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    It has been revealed that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    Sources indicate that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized customers to the card at no extra cost.

    Sources indicate that $99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

    The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

    As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:.

    Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

    It’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

    Industry observers note that rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    It has been revealed that basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Industry observers note that starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    Industry observers note that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

    Industry observers note that southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

    Another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

    According to recent reports, each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

    Sources indicate that on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

    According to recent reports, as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

    The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

    You’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

    However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

    In a recent development, if your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

    You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

    The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:.

    There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

    The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:.

    So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

    According to recent reports, if you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:.

    The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee.     Tech Report: Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Substantial Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire.
    • This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.
    • Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

    This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

    Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

    I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

    Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

    Recent findings suggest that stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

    I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an issue using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

    I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

    I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

    As such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to Newly introduced York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

    Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

    Sources indicate that neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

    Sources indicate that as a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

    I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

    For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

    Sources indicate that my experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this….

    According to recent reports, I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

    I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

    I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

    #191423. When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1452 w)

    When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that to push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question.
    • Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those).
    • The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that to push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices….

    Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

    The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

    In most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

    However, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

    While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

    Recent findings suggest that broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

    I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

    I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is currently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

    When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

    It’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

    Cathay Pacific first class is exactly the opposite — the crews are spectacularly reactive. That might sound sarcastic, but it’s not. On Cathay Pacific you (hopefully) won’t see a flight attendant once between meal services without calling them, and that’s so that your privacy is maximized. But if you push the call button a flight attendant will cheerily appear within seconds.

    Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

    Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

    Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:.

    That being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

    The above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:.

    In a recent development, on US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes issue with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

    Recent findings suggest that all airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no challenges with using them for service.

    Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

    Sources indicate that us airline here . I’m more than happy to take call lights in any cabin. When it gets concerning is when I customs keeps pressing it for alcohol refills . I have never heard crew members making an announcement that the call light is for emergency only , except when customer press it during taxi, take off , and landing.

    Who else ran to the comments to see how you crazy folk use the call button.

    I use it in business class if I'm done with a meal and am burried in the set table with plates and all. Without the call button the crew may not proactively come clear it for hours.

    If the airline offered complementary drinks, then no reason not to use it to ask for another. Just because they served you one doesn’t make a difference, there’s no cap on how many drinks are complementary so it’s part of the job. If the tray hasn’t been cleared and you need the bathroom. Yes you should feel comfortable calling the crew. If you want your meal early, that’s pushing it. You want an extra blanket? Maybe. You want to adjust the cabin temperature; I’d reserve this request for premium cabins, unless the temperature is ridiculous. Merely my opinion though, of course, now how it practically works - you will always get some cabin crew who don’t want to do extra work so even resent basic aspects of their job like serving drinks or clearing a table so you can, you know, get out of your seat to the bathroom - not really optional! I’m too hot/cold, I can’t wait to eat? Well that’s getting ridiculous. Even as a frequent F traveller I don’t expect them to rush a fine meal service just because I’m impatient. In an F cabin with say 3 other passengers, changing the cabin temperature should be done gracefully and only pushed back if other customers are opposing the request. I can see how this will play out totally differently in a cabin with 100 other passengers in close proximity.

    I do not care what cabin I’m travelling in, I’m pressing the button if I want something.

    Sources indicate that IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 300,000 points, pre-bonus.

    In a recent development, IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

    It has been revealed that therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

    It has been revealed that IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

    However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

    For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

    That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

    On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

    That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

    However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

    That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

    Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

    You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand Fresh IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

    That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

    In a recent development, just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

    Sources indicate that IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:.

    Industry observers note that everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

    For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

    According to recent reports, keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand Newly introduced IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

    IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

    According to recent reports, IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

    There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

    Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
    • It has been revealed that jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no declared opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    It has been revealed that jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no declared opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

    According to recent reports, while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    According to recent reports, “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get significant things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    Recent findings suggest that “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these challenges,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    “This is the beginning of a latest bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., noted at the press conference.

    Industry observers note that rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    It has been revealed that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the newly introduced majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    In a recent development, at his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    In a recent development, “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    It has been revealed that “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries stated Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he mentioned at his news conference.

    #191418. Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Points Everywhere

    Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Points Everywhere

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value.
    • I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right.
    • This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

    I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

    This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

    Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®.

    Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:.

    Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited currently has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

    Sources indicate that on the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    These intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

    According to recent reports, eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who at the moment have the card, or those who have received a newly introduced cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

    Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

    There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized consumers to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

    If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

    Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

    Industry observers note that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

    Industry observers note that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

    Sources indicate that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

    Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

    However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

    However, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:.

    In a recent development, with one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

    Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:.

    This can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

    Industry observers note that one thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

    While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:.

    That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

    In a recent development, for a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

    Recent findings suggest that with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for fresh purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

    With Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

    DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

    Sources indicate that the Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

    If you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

    I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    Sources indicate that I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

    For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:.

    It has been revealed that there are presently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

    It has been revealed that the cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

    In a recent development, chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

    Sources indicate that other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

    The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

    The Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

    Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

    Recent findings suggest that the reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

    The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

    Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

    According to recent reports, the downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

    So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

    It has been revealed that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

    The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the latest room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

    Industry observers note that dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points.     Industry observers note that after all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

    Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:.

    With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

    I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

    Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight: What your rights are in 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • Recent disruptions in U.S. air travel highlight the importance of understanding passenger refund rights.
  • Federal rules require airlines to issue refunds for canceled flights or significant delays if you choose not to travel, regardless of the cause.
  • A 'significant delay' is defined as three hours or more for domestic flights and six hours or more for international flights.
  • Refunds must be processed automatically and promptly—within seven days for credit card payments and 20 days for other payment methods.
  • Refund eligibility only applies if you decline rebooking and do not accept alternative compensation such as vouchers or miles.
  • Airlines are not required to provide compensation for meals, hotels or ground transportation unless the disruption is within their control.
  • Passengers can file a complaint with the Department of Transportation if they believe refund rules were not followed.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • In a recent development, I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet at the moment consists of 25 planes, including:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-newly introduced business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    In a recent development, I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an upgrade to reflect that.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet at the moment consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    The initiative is for the 787-9s to get all-fresh cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    Industry observers note that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

    We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Presently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the upcoming premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s upcoming premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-upcoming cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

    A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico).

    For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

    In a recent development, side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉.

    According to recent reports, while details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the fresh Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-newly introduced cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these fresh cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

    #191414. Where To Spot The Air France Airbus A318 Before It Finally Retires

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1438 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Where To Spot The Air France Airbus A318 Before It Finally Retires

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Air France's Airbus A318 was due to disappear from scheduled passenger service on November 8, but its retirement has been pushed back to March 27, 2027.
    • Using data from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, we analyzed 423 A318 flights between October 12 and November 8.
    • According to recent reports, the smallest member of the Airbus A320 family has already received several extensions to its service life with Air France.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Air France's Airbus A318 was due to disappear from scheduled passenger service on November 8, but its retirement has been pushed back to March 27, 2027. The airline's remaining aircraft are still operating from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), with Marseille (MRS), Toulouse (TLS), Bordeaux (BOD), Nice (NCE), Milan Linate (LIN), and Lyon (LYS) offering some of the most frequent opportunities to catch the type.

    Using data from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker, we analyzed 423 A318 flights between October 12 and November 8. The four aircraft visited 30 airports during those four weeks. One stopped appearing after October 20, although it has since returned to service. Their movements provide a useful indication of where and when to look, particularly for anyone planning a visit to Paris in the coming months.

    According to recent reports, the smallest member of the Airbus A320 family has already received several extensions to its service life with Air France. Last summer, the carrier extended planned A318 operations from November 8, 2026, until March 27, 2027. The revised timetable covers domestic French routes and a selection of intra-European destinations, with all the scheduled services operating through CDG.

    However, March 27 is the final date presently shown in the published schedule rather than a confirmed farewell flight. Aircraft assignments can also change independently of the route timetable, meaning the presence of an A318 in a booking system does not guarantee that passengers will actually travel on one. For spotters, recent movements are consequently more useful than relying entirely on flights advertised several months ahead.

    It has been revealed that air France has continued replacing its smaller A320-family aircraft with the Airbus A220-300. On November 6, the airline received its 60th A220, registered F-HOZJ, which subsequently entered passenger service on November 9. The new aircraft seats 148 passengers, compared with 131 on the A318, and is now used across much of the airline's European network. Nevertheless, the four remaining A318s continue to appear in daily operations.

    The busiest A318 route during our four-week analysis was between CDG and Marseille Provence Airport (MRS), with 69 recorded flights in both directions. Of these, 35 departed Paris and 34 returned from Marseille. Toulouse-Blagnac Airport (TLS) came second with 47 flights, followed by Bordeaux–Mérignac Airport (BOD) with 42. Together, these three domestic connections accounted for 158 flights, or more than a third of the total activity recorded.

    Sources indicate that nice Côte d'Azur Airport (NCE) was the fourth most frequently visited destination, with 28 flights. The leading international route was Milan Linate Airport (LIN), with 22, while Lyon–Saint Exupéry Airport (LYS) recorded 20. These six routes accounted for 228 of the 423 flights, making them the most useful starting points for anyone trying to photograph the aircraft away from CDG. The figures reflect actual recorded movements, not the number of A318 flights scheduled in the months ahead.

    In a recent development, marseille is particularly interesting because the A318 appeared on several different rotations rather than being restricted to a single flight number. AF7344 was recorded ten times from Paris during the analysis, while AF7336 appeared on eight departures. The late-evening AF7344 also operated with F-GUGP on November 21, according to subsequent flight history.

    In a recent development, despite their small number, the A318s were used across a geographically diverse network. We identified 30 different airports in 12 countries between October 12 and November 8, including CDG itself. France accounted for nine of these airports, while the aircraft also visited five in Italy, four in Spain, and two in Portugal. Outside these markets, the tracking data included destinations such as Amsterdam (AMS), Copenhagen (CPH), Warsaw (WAW), Munich (MUC), Prague (PRG), and Bergen (BGO).

    The aircraft were not limited to routes typically associated with the French domestic network. Recorded international flights include Paris to Casablanca Mohammed V International Airport (CMN), Málaga (AGP), and Ibiza Airport (IBZ). Bergen Airport (BGO) also appeared in the data, although each of these destinations was served far less frequently than the main domestic routes. A route appearing once or twice in four weeks should not be interpreted as a dependable spotting opportunity.

    Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, of the 423 recorded flights, 422 either departed from or arrived at CDG. The exception was a one-off flight between Bologna (BLQ) and Venice (VCE) on November 6. The French hub airport therefore remains the most obvious location for seeing one without having to predict its next destination, although the timing of a visit makes a substantial difference.

    As each of the active A318s generally completes around five flights on a flying day, the aircraft make repeated appearances at CDG throughout the day. Our tracking data contains 213 departures from the airport during the 28-day period, equivalent to an average of approximately eight daily departures across the remaining fleet. These were not evenly distributed across the day, however, and several periods offered considerably more activity than others.

    The most useful morning window was between 7:00 AM and 8:59 AM local time, when 49 A318 departures were recorded. Another 44 departures took place between noon and 1:59 PM, while 49 occurred between 6:00 PM and 9:59 PM. The later flights are less useful for photography during the winter months, although they provide additional opportunities for anyone primarily interested in watching or flying the aircraft.

    Particularly at CDG, it is worth following the registration rather than concentrating on just one scheduled departure. An A318 arriving from Bordeaux, Marseille, or Milan may continue to an entirely different destination after its turnaround. Watching the aircraft's inbound sector can therefore help establish whether the same airframe is likely to operate the next flight, rather than waiting for a single flight number that may be assigned another type.

    Four registrations appear in the four-week dataset: F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP. The busiest was F-GUGM, which completed 146 flights and was recorded on all 28 days. F-GUGO operated 129 flights across 26 days, while F-GUGN recorded 102 flights across 21 days after first appearing on October 19. On days when they flew, each aircraft generally operated around five sectors, although individual daily totals varied.

    According to recent reports, F-GUGP followed a different pattern as the aircraft completed 46 flights during the first nine days of the period, with its final recorded departure on October 20, when it flew from CDG to Casablanca. It did not appear again in our data through November 8. Consequently, the four-week figures primarily reflect the activity of three aircraft during the second half of the period, rather than a consistently deployed four-aircraft fleet.

    Industry observers note that more recent data indicates F-GUGP operating AF7344 from CDG to Marseille on November 21, departing at 8:15 PM and landing at 9:21 PM. Its return to flying demonstrates why a list of active registrations needs to be checked against current movements, particularly as the retirement date approaches.

    According to recent reports, the A318's wider route network may contain many possible destinations, but the availability of the actual aircraft will determine which services operate as planned. With only four registrations to follow, a single aircraft being unavailable can affect a sizeable proportion of the type's daily flying. That is also why an A318 shown against a route weeks in advance is not necessarily the aircraft that will turn up on departure day.

    According to recent reports, the easiest way to identify an A318 currently flying is to open the Simple Flying Live Flight Tracker and search for the aircraft type or one of the four registrations. F-GUGM, F-GUGN, F-GUGO, and F-GUGP provide a much narrower starting point than following every Air France flight from Paris. Filtering the map around CDG then makes it possible to see which aircraft are airborne and where they are heading.

    To find out where Air France's last A318s will fly, the most useful approach is to check the recent history of the individual aircraft and then compare it with the airline's upcoming flights. The four-week data suggests beginning with Marseille, Toulouse, and Bordeaux, before considering Nice, Milan Linate, or Lyon. However, the registration assigned on the day is more important than how often a particular route appears in October or early November.

    Industry observers note that found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    Recent findings suggest that the tracker also allows you to follow the aircraft without traveling to France, while registration-level histories reveal patterns that published schedules miss. When the final A318 flights take place, the same historical data should provide the most reliable record of which aircraft operated the last passenger service, rather than relying on the timetable alone.
