    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Industry observers note that trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one glitch with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    Recent findings suggest that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he remarked. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., remarked part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” stated Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump stated Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a massive reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, noted Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, mentioned he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine mentioned. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    It has been revealed that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    In a recent development, “Enforcement of the latest rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat mentioned, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    Sources indicate that “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    Recent findings suggest that he stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, stated Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    It has been revealed that trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the manufacturer’s president and CEO. He also noted he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Concerns at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    According to recent reports, “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear complications dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Latest York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is at the moment undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

    Recent findings suggest that as you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

    Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

    Recent findings suggest that JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:.

    The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

    It has been revealed that all things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

    Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

    So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:.

    Sources indicate that there is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

    Industry observers note that we know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

    Sources indicate that now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

    In a recent development, in terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the latest lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

    It has been revealed that the Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s upcoming lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia.
    • A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed aims to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan.
    • As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we know that Delta has huge growth aspirations across the Pacific, particularly to Asia. It’s an area where Delta has increasingly fallen behind United in recent years, but Delta now hopes to not only catch up, but even beat United. We’ll see what comes of that, and in particular, find out just how costly that growth is.

    A few months ago, Delta executives publicly confirmed aims to return to Singapore, a destination that hasn’t been served by the airline since 2019, when that was an intra-Asia tag flight from Japan. Executives also confirmed out of which airport the service would operate. There’s now an additional update, as an announcement about the latest route is imminent, which almost certainly points to a fall 2027 launch for the service.

    As Delta executives view it, the airline is pretty maxed out in terms of its European potential, and in the long run, they see the most long haul growth potential in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. So, what kind of expansion should we expect?

    Back in August 2026, Delta Chief Commercial Officer Joe Esposito explicitly confirmed that the airline would return to Singapore. What was perhaps most interesting is that he also indirectly confirmed the hub out of which the service would operate — Esposito ruled out that the service could operate out of Los Angeles, so it’s pretty clear that the airline will operate this service out of Seattle (SEA).

    That’s also what JonNYC reported in the past, and now we can take that a step further — Delta is holding an event in Seattle in early December 2026, and that’s when the airline is expected to announce the service.

    My guess is that we’re looking at a fall 2027 service start, at best. At 8,070 miles, this will be Delta’s third longest flight, after its routes to South Africa, which are from Atlanta (ATL) to Cape Town (CPT) and Johannesburg (JNB).

    One certainly wonders if this Singapore route could be operated by Delta’s latest Airbus A350-1000s, which will feature an all-new passenger experience. While the plane has great range and per seat economics, the only thing I’d say is that it’s “a lot of plane” for a new market, in terms of the overall capacity (even with the very premium layout).

    In both the Seattle and Los Angeles to Singapore market, Singapore Airlines is the only other carrier operating. So competitively there’s not a huge difference in that regard, though Los Angeles is a significantly larger market in terms of demand for Singapore, and for that matter, Singapore Airlines also has more service out of the airport. But perhaps Delta is also looking to beat Alaska to the punch in the Seattle market.

    Industry observers note that it’s fantastic to see Delta looking to grow its presence in Asia. Point-to-point flying to Asia is a market that United has basically had cornered in recent years, and competition is good for consumers.

    It’s amazing to think for how many years Delta basically squandered its Asia advantage. Keep in mind that back in the day, Northwest had a robust Asia network, and after the merger with Delta, we saw that network decreased slowly but steadily, as Delta instead focused on routing everything through Seoul Incheon, and into the Korean Air network. So I’m happy to see a reversal of that strategy.

    It has been revealed that I also have to say that given Delta’s hubris, it’s kind of fun to see the airline having to increasingly play “catch up,” rather than coming in as the dominant carrier. And I think that very much sums up what’s going on in Asia.

    Industry observers note that the most basic structural disadvantage that Delta has is that United has a fortress hub in San Francisco (SFO), which is where a large part of its Asia network flies from. That’s fantastic for connectivity, not to mention San Francisco is a very strong market for Asia traffic.

    Sources indicate that delta, meanwhile, is taking a split hub approach, flying out of both Los Angeles and Seattle. Obviously Delta is trying to make the best of its situation, but there’s no denying that this is an uphill battle:.

    It also has to be emphasized that in terms of actually transporting passengers profitably (or at less of a loss), United does a better job at that than Delta, despite its lower overall profitability. Comparing passenger revenue per air seat mile to cost per air seat mile, United is at 16.18 cents vs. 16.46 cents, while Delta is at 17.37 cents vs. 19.31 cents.

    Sources indicate that delta is growing quite a bit in Asia at the moment. The airline has already introduced flights to Hong Kong, with flights now on sale to Manila and Tokyo Narita. On top of that, Delta is expected to announce a new Seattle to Singapore route within the next two weeks, with a launch likely planned for the fall of 2027.

    In a recent development, it’s great for passengers to see more competition across the Pacific, as Delta sure is making up for a lack of effort for years. However, the airline will also have quite the disadvantage compared to United for a long time….

    American Airlines Drops Chicago Gate Lawsuit, But Doubles Down On Turf War With United

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines is dropping its lawsuit against the City of Chicago and United Airlines over the controversial redistribution of gates at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD).
    • It has been revealed that however, American is arguably in a stronger competitive position at O'Hare than when it first debuted its legal challenge.
    • Industry observers note that in a court filing dated November 20, as reported by View From The Wing, American requested that its entire complaint be dismissed with prejudice, meaning it would be unable to pursue the same claims again, including those for financial damages.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is dropping its lawsuit against the City of Chicago and United Airlines over the controversial redistribution of gates at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). The decision follows an unsuccessful appeal last week, bringing the carrier's 18-month legal battle over the allocation of airport infrastructure toward a close.

    It has been revealed that however, American is arguably in a stronger competitive position at O'Hare than when it first debuted its legal challenge. The airline has recovered gate space, significantly expanded its network, and announced further investments in its third-largest hub. Nevertheless, Reuters reports that United's continued dominance in Chicago presents a considerable obstacle to American's ambitions of rebuilding a profitable operation.

    Industry observers note that in a court filing dated November 20, as reported by View From The Wing, American requested that its entire complaint be dismissed with prejudice, meaning it would be unable to pursue the same claims again, including those for financial damages. Neither Chicago nor United opposes the motion, with each party bearing its own legal expenses under the proposed dismissal. American explained its decision in a statement to View From The Wing:.

    “We stand by our decision to advocate for a fair process, and today, we believe the best way to continue delivering on that commitment is to look ahead.”.

    According to recent reports, the dispute originated in O'Hare's 2018 Airline Use and Lease Agreement (AULA), which allows gates to be redistributed according to airlines' flight activity. American argued that delays in delivering additional gates in Concourse L meant that a contractually agreed expansion period had not been fulfilled, precluding any redistribution until 2027. Unsurprisingly, the City of Chicago and United disagreed.

    Chicago adopts a new lease agreement, allowing periodic gate redistribution based on airlines' shares of departures.

    According to recent reports, delta's relocation to Terminal 5 triggers a protected expansion period. American's anticipated additional Concourse L gates remain unavailable.

    At United's request, Chicago begins redistributing gate space based on 2024 flight activity.

    American sues Chicago in federal court, seeking to prevent redistribution until April 2027.

    Chicago finalizes the fresh allocations, with American losing four gates and United gaining five.

    Recent findings suggest that united joins the federal case, raising jurisdictional complications. American withdraws that case and files a state court complaint on July 16.

    Following a seven-day hearing, the court denies American's request for an injunction to block the redistribution.

    Sources indicate that the revised gate allocations take effect, strengthening United's position at O'Hare. American appeals the denial of its preliminary injunction.

    Chicago and United submit their formal responses to American's complaint.

    Proceedings on the underlying complaint are suspended pending resolution of the appeal.

    The appellate court upholds the injunction denial, citing the balance of harm to airlines, passengers and airport operations.

    American moves to permanently dismiss its complaint, including its outstanding damages claims.

    Sources: Illinois Appellate Court ruling, American's dismissal motion and Chicago Department of Aviation.

    Notably, the appellate court did not definitively determine whether Chicago had breached its contractual obligations. Rather, it concluded that the potential disruption from reversing the redistribution outweighed the harm that American faced. The airline could have continued pursuing compensation, but its commercial circumstances at O'Hare have changed considerably since it filed the original complaint.

    It has been revealed that american's aggressive expansion at O'Hare has already yielded tangible results. In June, Chicago confirmed that American had earned additional gate space through its increased flight activity, reversing much of the previous year's losses. Separately, the carrier strengthened its position by paying $30 million to acquire the preferential-use lease hold rights for gates G8 and G10 from Spirit Airlines under its Chapter 11 proceedings.

    United CEO Scott Kirby had previously vowed to prevent American from gaining further gates at United's expense, targeting 750 daily departures from Chicago. However, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) intervened over congestion concerns, forcing United to cut more than 100 daily departures. Reuters reports that those flight restrictions have subsequently been extended through October 2027, limiting United's ability to overwhelm American through additional frequencies.

    *Net gate position reflects four gates lost, three regained, and two acquired.

    According to recent reports, american's expansion has also strengthened Chicago's long-haul connectivity. The carrier released flights to Naples and Honolulu last year, with nonstop service to Maui commencing on December 17. Furthermore, its return to Tokyo Narita in March next year will give American its 11th long-haul route from O'Hare, underscoring its ambitions to rebuild Chicago as an international gateway.

    Despite American's progress, considerable financial and competitive challenges remain. United's faster post-pandemic recovery has enabled it to establish a substantial market share advantage. More concerningly, a Deutsche Bank analysis reported by Reuters in February highlighted the enormous disparity between the financial performance of the two airlines' respective Chicago operations.

    Estimated 2025 operating margin.

    Implied annual operating profit/loss.

    Industry observers note that united is also strengthening its customer proposition through its United Next fleet modernization program and the rollout of free Starlink connectivity, which is scheduled for fleetwide completion by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, O'Hare's infrastructure expansion will unlock significant additional growth opportunities, with 19 new gates in Concourse D in 2028 and a further 14 in Concourse E in 2030.

    Recent findings suggest that however, American is making substantial customer experience investments of its own. Its new Concourse L Admirals Club will open in 2027, doubling the existing lounge's footprint, while premium cabins are now available on every Chicago departure. Having successfully defended its ability to compete at O'Hare, American's next challenge will be translating its expanded presence and improved passenger experience into sustainable profitability.

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz remarked. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    According to recent reports, “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they remarked.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer stated they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

    It has been revealed that democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter mentioned.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related challenges,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Sources indicate that democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    Sources indicate that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

    Moran also mentioned he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    • In a recent development, while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

    News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused concerns for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

    In a recent development, while the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

    This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

    The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

    Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

    Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

    I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

    While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

    Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

    Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the glitch here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

    In a recent development, he attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

    Recent findings suggest that ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an patch, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

    The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

    This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss upcoming security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

    In a recent development, emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:.

    “The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the firm has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”.

    Sources indicate that tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

    Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

    However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

    I am curious if there were some newly introduced policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

    Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

    Recent findings suggest that some fresh security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

    This resumption is a massive deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

    Industry News: Here’s what Thanksgiving foods you can bring in your carry-on and what has to be checked

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.
    • But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are notable rules to know.
    • The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

    But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are notable rules to know.

    The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

    And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

    “It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

    That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

    Industry observers note that last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

    If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

    Read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist.

    As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

    If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

    Sources indicate that most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

    Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

    Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

    It has been revealed that that means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

    You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

    If you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

    Other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

    Industry observers note that with many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”.

    TSA officers have historically said that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

    Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

    According to recent reports, if your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

    In a recent development, every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

    Whether you strategy to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

    On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

    Industry News: Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (981 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • According to recent reports, in the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route released — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • In a recent development, what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    According to recent reports, in the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route released — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    In a recent development, what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    Sources indicate that this was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    The route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    Sources indicate that I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    According to recent reports, air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was rolled out in the first place, and is sticking around.

    While the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

    Latest Update: Why The US Military Is Expanding A Remote Pacific Airport To Reduce Its Reliance On Guam

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, in October and November, I visited the Micronesian island countries of Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM).
    • Sources indicate that when I visited, work on the airport had not yet started, and the US military footprint on the island was minimal.
    • In a recent development, the knowledge that Yap Island's airport was soon to be transformed was surreal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, in October and November, I visited the Micronesian island countries of Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). The FSM consists of four states: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae. I visited Yap, whose airport is set to receive some major work by the United States to prepare it for war as part of the USAF's broader Agile Combat Employment (ACE) doctrine to disperse aircraft from Guam. Separately, US Navy personnel on the island informed me that there are plans to dredge the island's harbor to allow large warships to berth. Funding has not yet been approved.

    Sources indicate that when I visited, work on the airport had not yet started, and the US military footprint on the island was minimal. The hotel I stayed at houses around half the personnel (mostly US Navy) on the island for periods of six months. I arrived in Yap from Palau, where the minor airfield of Peleliu was closed because major construction work to expand the airport for ACE operations was underway. Here is what to know about the US's aims to expand Yap International Airport to relieve wartime strain on Andersen Air Force Base in Guam.

    In a recent development, the knowledge that Yap Island's airport was soon to be transformed was surreal. The island is one of the remote islands in the Pacific and is difficult and expensive to reach. Adjacent to the international airport is an old Japanesee WWII airfield littered with aircraft destroyed by American bombing and lost to the jungle. I found around eight Japanese airplanes, some marked, some not marked. Here and there around the islands are the remains of lost US Vought F4U Corsairs and bombers.

    Industry observers note that today, the island feels like a world away, but the USAF aims to improve the airports and airfields on the Second Island Chain as competition with China heats up. The echoes from WWII are clear. In 1944, the US island-hopped to Japan to project airpower over the Japanese home islands.

    Sources indicate that now those same islands are needed to project airpower over the First Island Chain. The First Island Chain includes Taiwan, Japan's southern islands, and the Philippines. Following WWII, the US consolidated its airpower and military bases on Guam, while maintaining forward bases in Japan and Korea. The rise of China puts not only those forward bases at risk, but also Guam, which is now a prime target. Without Guam, or an effective alternative, the US's ability to project airpower over the region would diminish drastically.

    The WWII US invasion of the island of Peleliu was one of the deadliest operations for the US Marines during the Pacific War. Fortunately for the native Yapese, the island was not invaded. Instead, it was intensively bombed, bypassed, and rendered irrelevant. Japanese forces remained on the island until the surrender. Most of their aircraft were destroyed in air campaigns.

    In a recent development, the Japanese airfield is now abandoned and overgrown, but next to it, Yap International Airport operates. Yap Airport is a simple single-runway airport with a basic terminal building. The only scheduled passenger flights that use the airport are United Airlines and Pacific Missionary Aviation (PMA) United operates 737 MAX 8 flights from Guam twice weekly; this is the primary connection to the outside world. Outside of United's flights, Yap's terminal building is generally closed.

    PMA operates passenger flights once a week (soon to be twice) from neighboring Palau using its two Super King Airs (seven to nine seats, depending on freight). PMA also operates flights to Yap's outlying islands as well as MEDEVAC and emergency services. I flew the PMA passenger flight from Palau to Yap, was invited on a flight to an outlying island (Ulithi), and flew out on United. PMA operates from its own private hangar and operates domestic flights from there. International (Palau) flights run through the main terminal.

    Funding for Yap Airport's transformation appears in two main categories: civilian FAA Airport Improvement Program (AIP) grants and the Department of Defense/Air Force military construction and related funding. The Air Force's Fiscal Year 2025 Military Construction budget request included around $400 million for runway extension and related work. This is labeled "PDI: Runway Extension, Inc." in the documents. The first increment funding is $96 million.

    A modest reduction appears in Fiscal 2027 documents with the explanatory note, "Program execution encountered delays and slipped from FY2025 to FY2026, funding reflects the one-time decrease after increase to support acquisition of land for an agreed upon defense site under appropriate international agreement required to complete the runway extension, parking apron, and taxiway construction at Yap International Airport, Wake Island.".

    Sources indicate that the decrease is $31 million, but as the note includes Wake Island, it is unclear how much of this is relevant to Yap. The justification language for the funding emphasizes the need for a longer runway and facilities to support larger military aircraft for training, operations, contingency, and Agile Combat Employment. In the event of a high-end conflict with China, this likely means that Yap will be on China's list of strategic targets to be hit and neutralized.

    In a recent development, the United States is presently upgrading numerous airports and airfields across the Second Island Chain as part of its ACE doctrine and preparations to counter China. As stated, one of the most significant programs currently underway is rehabilitating Palau's Peleliu airfield, while Angaur Airfield is already complete. On Guam, the USAF is expanding parking areas on its primary Andersen Air Force Base and rehabilitating its adjacent, formerly abandoned Northwest Field.

    Sources indicate that one of the biggest areas of effort is on the island of Tinian in the Northern Mariana Islands. There, the USAF is expanding and rehabilitating Tinian International Airport and the formerly abandoned North Field. Nearby, the island of Rota (home to fewer than 2,000 inhabitants) has also been an area of interest and increased military exercises. The civil airports on Palau, Saipan, and Guam also factor into US ACE planning, even if no work is being carried out to expand them.

    Select Micronesian airports/airfields being expanded for ACE (per budget documents).

    One key effort is Australia. Australia is not part of the Second Island Chain, and the relationship with Washington is very different from that of small Pacific islands. In Australia, effort is mostly focused on Australia's northern RAAF bases: Tindal, RAAF Darwin, and possibly RAAF Amberley. These are being prepped primarily for US strategic bomber use with associated aerial tankers.

    According to recent reports, following WWII, the United States occupied the Japanese South Seas Mandate and formally took over administration as the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI). Eventually, the Trust Territory was broken up. The Northern Mariana Islands joined the United States as a commonwealth, while Palau, the FSM, and the Marshall Islands became independent nations with full United Nations membership.

    However, sovereignty for these islands is nuanced. As part of the process, the newly independent states signed the Compacts of Free Association with the United States. Of interest to this article is that the United States retained responsibility for the defense of the islands. In practical terms, this gives the US military the benefits of basing in US territories without the islands actually being US territories.

    The FSM government states, "Under the Compact, the United States provides financial assistance, defends the FSM’s territorial integrity, and allows FSM citizens unrestricted travel to the U.S. In return, the FSM grants the United States exclusive access to its land and waterways for strategic purposes." The Compact grants the United States "full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters," although in practice, the US extensively collaborates with the government rather than dictates.

    Visiting Yap today, it is surreal to feel so isolated and yet also see the island reprising its role as potentially returning to the frontline of a major Pacific competition. In the years ahead, the airport may start to see the deployment of US tankers and F-35 fighter jets just hundreds of feet (meters) away from the rusting hulks of Japanese Zeros and American Corsairs rotting in the jungle.

    In WWII, the US Navy drew up a initiative to invade Yap, but this was scrapped in favor of bombarding it and bypassing it. China’s primary counter to ACE is the continued expansion of the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force (PLARF) and supporting systems, including large inventories of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hypersonic missiles. These are intended to hold US airfields at risk across the First and Second Island Chains.

    It has been revealed that the US is aware of this. Increasingly, the US Air Force, Marines, and Navy are focusing on increasing the range of next-generation fighter jets (e.g., F-47 and F/A-XX). Logistics and assault requirements increasingly focus on being runway-independent, with the US Army's incoming MV-75 tiltrotor being an example. The Marines, in particular, are investing in a range of runway-independent and sea-skimming drone options for the 'last mile' of resupply and MEDEVAC.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • In a recent development, saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Sources indicate that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders noted Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Sources indicate that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Sources indicate that sanders remarked Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    It has been revealed that sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion strategy, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., mentioned last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    Breaking: Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase.
    • Recent findings suggest that this is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Recent findings suggest that this is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:.

    According to recent reports, if you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

    The Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

    Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who presently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    This is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

    Recent findings suggest that when it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being mentioned, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

    The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

    The card also has no extra cost to add authorized people, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

    The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    It has been revealed that for a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    Industry observers note that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    It has been revealed that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

    The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:.

    Recent findings suggest that personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

    Sources indicate that as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    In a recent development, as Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

    In a recent development, southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

    Sources indicate that preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

    Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

    According to recent reports, keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

    The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

    With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

    With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

    Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

    Recent findings suggest that on your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

    Industry observers note that in other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

    Industry observers note that if you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

    The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

    According to recent reports, many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

    According to recent reports, that stated, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

    First, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

    Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:.

    The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

    According to recent reports, there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:.

    I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

    Industry observers note that if you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:.

    According to recent reports, chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

    Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

    For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:.

    On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:.

    When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

    If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

    Industry observers note that if you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.
